settings.content: Ten silhouettes, and the hidden details that lift them

settings.eyebrow: The Shape of the Whole Ring
settings.heading: Style Is the Silhouette, Not the Setting
settings.body:
An engagement ring style describes how the whole ring is composed around its centre stone: whether that stone stands alone, sits inside a halo, is flanked by two others, or is framed by a rim of metal. It is the thing you recognise across a room.

That is a different question from how each individual stone is held in the metal, which is covered in stone settings and matters most on bands where stones repeat around the finger.

The style you choose changes three things at once: how large the centre stone reads on the hand, how the ring will sit against a future wedding band, and how much day-to-day care it will ask for.

settings.label: Solitaire
settings.heading: Solitaire, Plain Shoulders
settings.body: The timeless single-stone silhouette. Puts almost the entire budget into the stone, sits flush against most wedding bands, and suits every hand. Browse solitaires.

settings.label: Solitaire
settings.heading: Solitaire, Diamond Shoulders
settings.body: A classic solitaire with brilliant shoulders. More sparkle across the finger without enlarging the centre stone, though it limits future resizing slightly.

settings.label: Halo
settings.heading: Halo, Plain Shoulders
settings.body: Haloed presence on a clean band. A halo makes a centre stone read noticeably larger for the money, which is why it is the best-value way to buy visual size. Browse halos.

settings.label: Halo
settings.heading: Halo, Diamond Shoulders
settings.body: Halo and pavé shoulders together, for maximum sparkle. The brightest of the classic silhouettes, and the one that asks for the most regular inspection.

settings.label: Halo
settings.heading: Hidden Halo
settings.body: A secret halo seen only from the side. Clean from above, a surprise in profile, and a way to add sparkle without changing the ring's outline. Browse hidden halos.

settings.label: Multi-stone
settings.heading: Trilogy
settings.body: Three stones for past, present and future. Reads wider on the finger than a solitaire of the same total weight, and carries obvious meaning. Browse trilogy rings.

settings.label: Shoulders
settings.heading: Split Shoulders
settings.body: A divided band lifts and frames the stone, adding presence without adding carat weight. Often needs a shaped wedding band to sit flush.

settings.label: Multi-stone
settings.heading: Multistone Invisible
settings.body: Edge-to-edge stones with no visible metal between them. Modern and unusually bright, and quite unlike anything traditional. Browse invisible-set rings.

settings.label: Openwork
settings.heading: Oyster Deluxe
settings.body: An openwork basket cradles the stone, letting light in from beneath and lightening the whole design. Beautiful at close range.

settings.label: Protective
settings.heading: Bezel
settings.body: A full metal rim, sleek and secure. The most protective silhouette there is and the most snag-free, which makes it the sensible choice for hands-on work.

settings.heading: Ten Silhouettes, Compared
settings.intro: Illustrated at a consistent scale so the outlines can be judged honestly against each other.

settings.heading: Find Your Style by Priority
settings.intro: If you only know one thing about what matters most, start from that and work back.

settings.heading: Hidden halo
settings.body: Tiny diamonds tucked beneath the centre stone, visible only from the side. Clean from above, a private detail in profile.

settings.heading: Milgrain edging
settings.body: A row of tiny beaded metal dots along an edge. Characteristic of vintage and art-deco design, and it softens a hard line beautifully.

settings.heading: Gallery work and filigree
settings.body: Intricate metalwork beneath the head of the ring, seen only at close range. The part a jeweller judges another jeweller on.

settings.heading: Surprise diamonds
settings.body: Small accent stones set inside the band or under the basket, where only the wearer knows they are there.

settings.heading: Custom engraving
settings.body: A date, initials, a coordinate or a private phrase inside the band. Ask before the ring is finished, since some designs are harder to engrave afterwards.

settings.heading: Cathedral shoulders
settings.body: The band sweeps upward to meet the setting, lifting the stone and giving the profile an arched line rather than a flat one.

settings.heading: Hidden Details That Elevate a Ring
settings.intro: These cost comparatively little and are what people notice years later.

settings.cells: Hands-on or active | Bezel, low-profile solitaire | Secure and snag-free above all
Desk-based or creative | Almost anything | Halo, pavé and trilogy all wear well
Hands in water often | Bezel or low-profile platinum | Avoid softer stones entirely
Vintage lovers | Halo, hidden halo, milgrain and filigree | Detail rewards close looking
Minimalists | Solitaire, east-west, bezel | A plain band with a stand-out stone

settings.heading: Style by Lifestyle
settings.intro: A surgeon, a climber and a graphic designer all need different rings. A delicate vintage halo on a hands-on hand will catch, snag and eventually break.

settings.heading: Will a Wedding Band Sit Against It?
settings.body:
A spectacular engagement ring that will not sit flush with any straight band is a costly oversight, and one we see regularly. Low solitaires and bezels pair with almost anything. Split shoulders, cathedral settings and low-set halos often need a shaped or fitted band made to follow their outline.

It is far cheaper to know this before the engagement ring is made than to discover it a year later. Tell us if a matching band matters and we will design for the pair from the start.

settings.eyebrow: The Other Half of the Question
settings.heading: How the Stones Are Actually Held
settings.body: Style is the silhouette. How each individual stone is secured in the metal, claw, pavé, channel, bezel or flush, is a separate decision that governs sparkle, security and whether the ring can ever be resized.

settings.q: Which engagement ring style makes a diamond look biggest?
settings.a: A halo, comfortably. Surrounding the centre stone with small diamonds can add the appearance of half a carat or more for a fraction of the cost of buying that weight in the centre stone. A hidden halo does the same job more subtly.

settings.q: Which style is best if they work with their hands?
settings.a: Bezel, or a low-profile solitaire. Both keep the stone close to the finger with nothing to catch. A high claw setting on a busy hand will snag, and eventually a claw will bend or break.

settings.q: Will a wedding band sit flush against any of these?
settings.a: Low solitaires and bezels usually pair with a straight band without a gap. Split shoulders, cathedral settings and some halos leave a gap and want a shaped or fitted band. Decide early, because it is much easier to design the pair together.

settings.q: What is the difference between a halo and a hidden halo?
settings.a: A visible halo rings the centre stone when seen from above and makes it read larger. A hidden halo sits underneath the centre stone and is only visible from the side, so the ring keeps a clean outline while gaining sparkle in profile.

settings.q: Is a trilogy ring more expensive than a solitaire?
settings.a: Not necessarily. Three smaller stones can cost less than one large one of the same total weight, because price rises steeply with individual stone size. A trilogy often reads wider on the finger for less money.

Yes, and most bespoke commissions do. A hidden halo on a cathedral solitaire with milgrain edging is three ideas in one ring. Every design goes through a 3D CAD render first so you can see it before we cast, and edits are free.
